Vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Vinh Tran

Vinh Tran was thirty-one when he sought help, though his wife had been urging him to do so for nearly eighteen months. He sat in the consultation room with the careful posture of someone accustomed to maintaining composure in public—his judicial bearing intact even as he described the moment his life had fractured.

Two years earlier, Vinh had been visiting his parents in their home in the coastal town where he'd grown up. It was late August, and a tropical storm had been tracking toward the region for days. He remembered the news coverage, the warnings, the sense of mild concern that had felt manageable. On the morning the storm hit, he was helping his father secure the house when the wind shifted violently. Within minutes, the storm surge came with terrifying speed. He was caught in the garage as water began pouring in, rising faster than seemed possible. The sound was deafening—the roar of water, the shriek of metal, the crack of wood. He could taste salt and something chemical in the water. The light had taken on a sickly gray-green quality as debris churned in the murk around him. He had managed to reach a shelf, clinging there as the water rose, certain he would drown. The smell—a mixture of seawater, gasoline, and something acrid from damaged infrastructure—had filled his nostrils and throat. The whole event lasted perhaps eight minutes, though it had felt like hours. His father had pulled him out through a high window. No one died, but the house was destroyed.

In the months immediately following, Vinh had functioned. He returned to his position on the district court bench. He told people he was fine. But something had shifted in how the world felt to him. By October, when the autumn rains began, he found himself unable to leave the house on days when the weather resembled that August morning—overcast skies, a particular humidity in the air, the threat implicit in gray clouds. His wife, Linh, would mention a work obligation or a family dinner, and he would feel his chest tighten. The thought of being outside, exposed to weather that might turn, felt impossible. He began finding reasons not to go.

The triggers accumulated and branched. An ambulance siren near the courthouse made his entire body go rigid; his mind would flash with the image of that gray-green water, the shelf he'd clung to, and he would be gasping as though drowning again. The hospital smell—that sharp, antiseptic tang—caught him off guard once when he visited a colleague. He'd had to excuse himself, his heart racing, sweat pouring down his face. He was certain that if he allowed himself to relax, to let his guard down, something catastrophic would happen. Relaxation felt like a luxury he could no longer afford, a dangerous indulgence. He began sleeping poorly, his body tense through the night. When he did manage to sleep, the dreams came—not narrative dreams, but vivid, sensory snapshots. He would see the water rising, the gray-green light, the shelf beneath his hands. Each image was crystalline, frozen, but when they came, they came with the full force of sensation: the cold water, the salt taste, the chemical smell, the sound of rushing destruction. It felt completely real, as though he were there again, drowning in real time.

He had tried, in those early months, to push the memories away. Whenever the images began to surface, he would force his attention elsewhere—work documents, news articles, anything to fill his mind. But the effort was exhausting, and the memories would return with greater intensity, as though they had been building pressure behind a dam. His avoidance had spread. He stopped going to the courthouse gym. He declined invitations from colleagues. He found himself leaving the bench early on days when the weather looked uncertain. Linh had begun to withdraw, hurt and confused. His relationship with her had grown distant; they occupied the same house but lived in separate spheres. She had finally insisted that he speak to someone, that something was seriously wrong.

Vinh came to the appointment because his wife had made it clear it was necessary, not because he believed anything could help. What frightened him most was the possibility that he might lose control, that the memories would overwhelm him completely and he would be unable to function as a judge, as a husband, as the person he had worked his entire life to become. He was hoping, though he barely allowed himself to articulate it, that someone could help him understand why his own mind had become dangerous to him.
